newsitem.title: USA: Dole meets Netanyahu, calls for end to violence.
newsitem.headline: Dole meets Netanyahu, calls for end to violence.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole sounded a sour note on the Middle East summit on Wednesday, saying it demonstrated that the United States cannot impose a solution.

In a short statement issued minutes after a half-hour meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Dole criticised President Bill Clinton for not unequivocally condemning the recent violence when he brought to an end the talks between Netanyahu, Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat and Jordan's King Hussein in Washington.

But Dole, the former Senate majority leader who on Tuesday called the summit another example of Clinton "photo-op" foreign policy, declined to go into detail during a brief photo-op he had with Netanyahu before the two men began their talks as self-described "old friends."
When asked by reporters what he would have done, Dole said his statement would reflect his feelings.
He was silent when asked if he agreed with U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, who called the summit a failure.
Netanyahu said he was not taking sides in the U.S. election by meeting Dole, adding, "I don't get involved in domestic disputes."

In his statement Dole said he stressed in his talks with Netanyahu "our shared belief that violence is not an acceptable means of resolving differences. Violence must not be rewarded. Therefore the most important objective at the present time is to end the violence -- unconditionally."
He added, "I was disappointed that President Clinton's statement did not include an unequivocal condemnation of the recent violence. ....

"As the Washington summit demonstrated, the United States cannot impose a solution. However, we can stand clearly in support of peaceful resolution of differences between the Israelis and the Palestinians and truly just peace."
Dole has been trying to walk a fine line on foreign policy, trying both to support American policy in times of crisis while presenting himself as better able to handle foreign policy than Clinton.
